newsitem.title: USA: US red winter wheat production seen up in report.
newsitem.headline: US red winter wheat production seen up in report.

text.p: Favorable growing weather after a spring freeze in the U.S. hard red winter wheat belt is likely to prompt the U.S. Department of Agriculture to boost its 1997 winter wheat production forecast, grain analysts said.

"I think we shivered the plants a little bit but afterwards, the weather was ideal, said Sid Love, grain analyst with Kropf and Love consulting. "It was cool and wet and I never did feel that those losses were justified."

On Friday, USDA will release winter and spring wheat production estimates. Analysts are most focused on the hard red winter wheat crop, which is currently being harvested in Kansas and Oklahoma, Texas and parts of Nebraska.
Much of the crop was thought to have been damaged by a freeze in April, but yields so far have been good and some industry sources are predicting a record crop for Kansas.
An average of analysts' estimates put the hard red winter wheat production at 1.000 billion bushels. That figure compared to USDA's June production estimate of 921 million bushels.
Soft red winter wheat production was seen at 431 million bushels, and total winter wheat was seen at 1.687 billion, according to the averages of analysts' estimates.
Early results from the soft red winter wheat harvest have also been favorable and most analysts see that crop surpassing USDA's previous estimate of 422 million bushels.
"Yields in Arkansas have been huge, and as you get up around St. Louis, yields have also been good," Love said. "All you can say is that we've got to add more bushels."
A grain dealer for a major Midwest firm said that all of the new crop soft wheat received at his terminal was of high quality.
Test weights from Illinois, Indiana and southern Ohio have mostly been 58 lbs per bushel or higher and yields of 70 to 90 bushels per acre were common, cash sources said.
"We do not detect any vomotoxin or aflatoxin. It looks like a pretty clean crop," the dealer said.
Harvest in central Ohio and northern Indiana was about a week away, but so far the crop was healthy and was expected to produce high yields and test weights, cash dealers there said.
Estimates for spring wheat production ranged widely because conditions in the spring wheat states have been highly variable, analysts said.
"I think you'll have some areas where you have record yields, and other areas where they've turned it over to the insurance people," said Doug Hjort, president of Hjort and Associates in Adel, Iowa.

Analysts' estimates for other spring wheat production ranged from 590 million to 702 million bushels, with the average estimate at 634 million. In 1996, USDA put the spring wheat crop at 688 million bushels.

The spring wheat in north central Montana looks very good, but in northeastern North Dakota, acres have been torn up because the rains that fell were too heavy and fast to be absorbed by the wheat, Hjort said.
"They've gotten an inch or two of rain in two hours time," Hjort said. "That's pretty hilly country away from the Red River Valley, and it just washes away.
Other analysts saw recent rains as largely beneficial for the spring wheat crop.

"I'm at the high side of the estimates because I believe that the timely rains we've seen out there will increase hard red spring yields," said Tom Levis, analyst with Prudential Securities in Chicago.
